passage:
Tuesday. Another magazine piece about our startup, and Devika's photo is the big one. Devika's name is in the headline, mine in the fifth paragraph. Investors keep emailing Devika. At the launch party I smiled and congratulated everyone, and in the taxi I felt small and bitter and invisible. Today I even caught myself "forgetting" to forward Devika an email. That's exactly what I don't want to become.

Wednesday. I told Devika: "When articles and investors go only to you, I feel invisible, and I've been sulking instead of saying so." Devika went quiet, then said they hadn't noticed. We wrote down who speaks to the press, who speaks to investors, and that the next feature names both of us. The sting is still there, but it's cleaner now.

Wasim

qa.q: Whose name is in the headline of the magazine piece?
qa.a: Devika's name is in the headline.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel in the taxi after the launch party?
What did Wasim do to deal with the envy?
qa.a: Wasim told Devika directly, and they agreed who speaks to the press and to investors and that the next feature names both.

qa.q: How might Devika have experienced Wasim's words?
qa.a: Devika went quiet and said they hadn't noticed, suggesting Devika had been unaware of Wasim's feelings rather than ignoring them.

grounding: A co-founder gets the media credit and investor attention and Wasim feels invisible and bitter; Wasim says so directly and agrees fair credit and roles.

passage:
"Did you see the newspaper piece?" Rajni asked, bright-eyed, holding up her phone. "'The young woman who put millets on every tiffin.'"

"I saw." Kashish kept stirring the test batch.

"You're quiet."

"I'm fine."

"Kashish."

Kashish put down the ladle. "Okay. I'm not fine. I built the whole supply chain. I found the farmers. And every article is about you. The investors only look at you. I've been feeling invisible. And bitter, honestly. Last week I nearly didn't send you the sales figures before your interview."

Rajni's face fell. "I didn't know. I just... answer when they call."

"I know. That's why I'm saying it to you, not to anyone else."

Rajni sat on the stool. "So what's fair?"

"Both our names in every press note. I take the investor calls on operations. And we decide together who speaks."

"Done," Rajni said. "And Kashish, thank you for telling me."

qa.q: What did the newspaper piece call Rajni?
qa.a: It called her "The young woman who put millets on every tiffin."

qa.q: What had Kashish been feeling about the articles?
qa.a: Kashish had been feeling invisible and bitter, even tempted to hold back the sales figures.

qa.q: Why was telling Rajni directly the right choice?
qa.a: Saying it openly let them agree fair credit and roles, instead of Kashish quietly undermining her.

qa.q: How did Rajni see the situation before Kashish spoke?
qa.a: Rajni hadn't noticed; she thought she was simply answering when journalists called.

grounding: A dialogue shows a co-founder who feels invisible and bitter when the other partner gets the media credit, who says it directly and agrees on fair credit and roles.

passage:
I'm Sahil, and I'll admit this: when the investor at the demo day shook Pranav's hand and walked right past mine, I wanted to trip him.

Pranav is the face of our ed-tech startup. He's good on stage. I write the code that makes the thing work. For a year, every podcast, every panel, every photo was him. I started feeling like furniture. And bitter.

The worst part was what I began doing. I stopped telling him about bugs until the last minute. Once, I let him walk into a pitch with an old slide. I told myself I was busy.

That night I saw it plainly: I was sabotaging my own company to punish my friend.

The next day I asked Pranav for coffee and said all of it, even the slide. He was quiet, then said, "You should be on stage too." We agreed: I present the product, he presents the vision, and both our names go on everything.

qa.q: What did Sahil let Pranav walk into a pitch with?
qa.a: Sahil let him walk into a pitch with an old slide.

qa.q: What was Sahil feeling as Pranav got all the attention?
qa.a: Sahil felt invisible, like furniture, and bitter enough to want to trip Pranav.

qa.q: What did Sahil do once he saw what he was doing?
qa.a: Sahil told Pranav everything directly, including the slide, and they agreed fair roles and shared credit.

qa.q: How did Pranav respond to Sahil's honesty?
qa.a: Pranav took it quietly and generously, suggesting Sahil should be on stage too.

grounding: A first-person account shows a co-founder envious of a partner's credit who notices the urge to undermine him, then speaks directly and agrees fair credit and roles.
